common_name: Seyval Blanc Grape (Cold-Hardy French-American White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or potted vines in early spring once soil is workable, training to a trellis or arbor with a permanent trunk and cane or cordon system.

directions: This French-American hybrid produces tight clusters of small green-white berries used for crisp, high-acid white wine and is valued in cooler regions where vinifera struggle to ripen. It shows good resistance to downy and powdery mildew compared to vinifera but is prone to bunch rot in humid climates, so canopy management and cluster thinning improve air circulation. Prune to a cane or cordon system and expect vines to reach full production by the third or fourth year. It is more cold-hardy than most vinifera, tolerating winter lows that would damage traditional wine grapes.
sources: Missouri State University Grape and Wine Institute

common_name: Cayuga White Grape (Cornell-Bred Disease-Resistant White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Set dormant vines in early spring in well-drained soil, spacing plants for a trellised row and training to a bilateral cordon or cane system.

directions: Released by Cornell's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in 1972 from a Seyval x Schuyler cross, this hybrid combines good winter hardiness with strong resistance to black rot and mildew, making it a reliable choice for home vineyards in humid eastern climates. Clusters of pale green-white grapes work well for both fresh eating and light, fruity white wine. Vines are moderately vigorous and benefit from cluster thinning to avoid overcropping, which can delay ripening. It buds out relatively late in spring, giving some protection from late frosts.
sources: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Baco Noir Grape (French-American Hybrid Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant vines in early spring in well-drained soil, training young vines up a stake to the trellis wire in their first season.

directions: Bred in France from a Folle Blanche x Vitis riparia cross, this hybrid produces small dark berries that make a deeply colored, earthy red wine and has long been favored in cool-climate wine regions for its reliable ripening in cool seasons. It shows strong resistance to downy mildew and better cold tolerance than most vinifera, though it can be vigorous and needs regular canopy management to prevent overcrowding. The wine has a distinctive herbal, smoky character that mellows with age. Vines typically reach full bearing by their fourth year.
sources: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs

common_name: De Chaunac Grape (Cold-Hardy French-American Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Set dormant vines in early spring once soil can be worked, training to a cane or cordon trellis system with a sturdy permanent trunk.

directions: Named for the Canadian winemaker who popularized it, this hybrid was once one of the most widely planted French-American varieties in the Finger Lakes and Ontario before newer hybrids surpassed it, but it remains a dependable, productive vine for home growers wanting a cold-hardy red. It produces heavy crops of small blue-black berries that yield a soft, fruity red wine and needs cluster thinning to avoid overbearing and delayed ripening. The vine tolerates winter cold better than vinifera and resists downy mildew reasonably well but can be susceptible to bunch rot in wet autumns. Prune moderately hard each dormant season to balance vigor and fruit quality.
sources: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs

common_name: Noiret Grape (Cornell-Bred Disease-Resistant Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant vines in early spring in well-drained soil, training to a cordon-trained trellis and staking the trunk in the first year.

directions: Released by Cornell's breeding program in 2006 from complex hybrid parentage including Steuben and Chancellor, this variety produces small dark-skinned berries that yield a deeply colored, peppery red wine with good tannin structure for a hybrid. It buds late, which helps it dodge spring frost damage, and shows strong resistance to fungal diseases common in humid eastern vineyards. Vines are vigorous and benefit from shoot thinning early in the season to manage canopy density and improve fruit ripening. It ranks among the more cold-hardy options for growers wanting a serious hybrid red rather than a juice or fresh-eating grape.
sources: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: St. Croix Grape (Extreme Cold-Hardy Red Wine and Juice Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant vines in early spring after the ground can be worked, training up a stake to the trellis and mulching to conserve moisture the first year.

directions: Bred by Minnesota grape breeder Elmer Swenson, this early-ripening hybrid tolerates winter temperatures well below zero without significant cane damage, making it a staple for northern growers who cannot overwinter vinifera or many other hybrids. Clusters of medium blue-black berries ripen early in the season and are used for both juice and light red wine with a mild, fruity character. The vine is naturally productive and needs cluster thinning in its early years to avoid overcropping, which can stunt future growth. Its combination of cold hardiness and early ripening makes it a dependable choice for short-season gardens.

common_name: Petite Pearl Grape (Cold-Hardy Dark Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant vines in early spring in well-drained soil, training to a cordon system and staking the young trunk for support.

directions: Bred by Minnesota grape breeder Tom Plocher and released in 2010, this hybrid produces small clusters of tiny, thick-skinned dark berries that concentrate color and tannin for a deeply pigmented red wine unusual among cold-hardy hybrids. It combines strong winter hardiness with good resistance to fungal disease, and its naturally low yields concentrate flavor without extensive crop thinning. The compact clusters also reduce bunch rot risk in humid seasons. It has become popular among small-scale and hobby winemakers in the northern United States seeking a hybrid capable of real varietal red wine character.

common_name: Louise Swenson Grape (Cold-Hardy White Wine and Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant vines in early spring once soil is workable, training young growth up a stake to reach the trellis wire.

directions: Named for the wife of Minnesota breeder Elmer Swenson, this hybrid produces large clusters of pale green-white berries with a mild, fruity flavor suited to fresh eating as well as aromatic white wine. It is one of the more cold-hardy white hybrids available, tolerating harsh northern winters that would kill vinifera vines outright. The loose cluster architecture helps reduce bunch rot in humid climates, and the vine is moderately vigorous, benefiting from a cordon or cane training system. Home growers in short-season regions value it for combining table-grape appeal with reliable hardiness.

common_name: Brianna Grape (Aromatic Cold-Hardy White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant vines in early spring in well-drained soil, training to a cordon or cane system with a stake for the young trunk.

directions: Developed by Elmer Swenson, this cold-hardy white hybrid produces medium clusters of golden-green berries with a distinctive tropical, pineapple-like aroma that carries into its wine, setting it apart from most other cold-climate whites. It ripens relatively late for a hardy hybrid but withstands harsh northern winters with minimal cane damage. The vine is vigorous and productive, often needing shoot positioning and crop thinning to maintain fruit quality and avoid overcropping. It has become a popular blending or single-varietal choice among small wineries across the upper Midwest.

common_name: Frontenac Gris Grape (Cold-Hardy Gray-Skinned White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant vines in early spring once soil is workable, training to a cordon or cane system on a sturdy trellis.

directions: This gray-skinned bud sport of Frontenac was released by the University of Minnesota and shares its parent's exceptional riparia-derived cold hardiness while producing an aromatic white wine with notes of apricot and citrus rather than Frontenac's deep red. It buds and ripens on a similar schedule to standard Frontenac and shows the same strong resistance to fungal disease and winter injury. Fruit can develop high sugar levels for late-harvest or dessert-style wines if left on the vine, though growers should watch for excessive acid drop in warm years. Like its parent, it benefits from cluster thinning to balance yield against flavor concentration.
